lessons.title: Git Basics: Snapshots and Commits
lessons.description: Understand what Git tracks and create your first commit

theorySlides.title: What is Git? 🌱
theorySlides.content:
Git is a version control system. Think of it as a time machine for your project:

• Save checkpoints (commits)
• Go back safely
• Compare changes
• Collaborate without overwriting each other

theorySlides.title: The 3 Core States
theorySlides.content:
In beginner Git, you can imagine 3 layers:

1) Working files (what you edit)
2) Staging area (what you prepare)
3) Commit history (what you save forever)
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
git status
# see current state

git add .
# stage all current changes

git commit -m "Initial layout"

theorySlides.title: First Commit Flow
theorySlides.content: A commit is a snapshot. Small, clear commits make projects easier to understand.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
git init
git status
git commit -m "Initial commit"

questions.question: What is the main purpose of Git?
questions.explanation: Git is for tracking file changes over time and coordinating work safely.

questions.question: What does a commit represent?
questions.explanation: A commit is a saved snapshot of your code at a specific moment.

questions.question: Which command creates a commit?
questions.explanation: Use git commit with a message to create a new snapshot in history.

questions.question: Why should commit messages be clear?
options: They help teammates understand what changed
questions.explanation: Good commit messages make project history readable for you and your team.

lessons.title: Branches: Isolated Work
lessons.description: Create and switch branches to work safely in parallel

theorySlides.title: Why Branches Matter 🌿
theorySlides.content:
Branches let you test ideas without breaking your main line:

• main stays stable
• feature branches hold experiments
• merging later combines finished work

theorySlides.title: Create and Move
theorySlides.content: Use branch + checkout (or checkout -b) to create isolated workspaces.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
git branch feature/login
git checkout feature/login
# now commits go to feature/login

theorySlides.title: Shortcut: checkout -b
theorySlides.content: Create and switch in one command. Great for fast feature starts.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
git checkout -b feature/navbar
git commit -m "Add navbar structure"

questions.question: What is the best reason to use a feature branch?
questions.explanation: Branches isolate unfinished work and protect the stable branch.

questions.question: What does git checkout -b feature do?
options: Creates and switches to feature branch
questions.explanation: checkout -b is a shortcut for branch creation + switch.

questions.question: After checkout to feature, where do new commits go?
questions.explanation: Commits are attached to the currently checked-out branch.

questions.question: Why keep main clean while learning?
options: To keep stable progress and avoid confusion
questions.explanation: A clean main branch makes project history and releases safer.

codingChallenge.title: Create and advance a feature branch
codingChallenge.description: Create a commit on main, then move to feature and create one more commit there.
codingChallenge.starterCode:
# 1) Make a baseline commit on main
# 2) Create feature branch
# 3) Switch to feature
# 4) Create a feature commit

testCases.input: Goal: finish on feature branch with separate tips for main and feature.
testCases.expectedOutput:
HEAD=feature
HAS_BRANCH=main
HAS_BRANCH=feature
MIN_COMMITS=3
BRANCH_AT=main:C1
BRANCH_AT=feature:C2
BRANCHES_DIFFER=main:feature

codingChallenge.hint: Sequence: git commit -> git branch feature -> git checkout feature -> git commit
codingChallenge.solution:
git commit -m "Base commit on main"
git branch feature
git checkout feature
git commit -m "Feature work"

lessons.title: Merge Fundamentals
lessons.description: Bring finished feature work back into main using merge commits

theorySlides.title: What is Merge? 🔀
theorySlides.content:
Merging combines histories from two branches.

When both branches moved, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

theorySlides.title: Basic Merge Workflow
theorySlides.content: You usually merge into main after feature work is ready.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
git checkout main
git merge feature
# main now includes feature history

theorySlides.title: Think in Graphs
theorySlides.content: Git is a commit graph, not a folder copy. Branch names are movable labels pointing at commits.

questions.question: What does git merge feature do from main?
options: Moves feature to main without history
questions.explanation: Merge integrates another branch history into the current branch.

questions.question: Where should you be before merging feature into main?
questions.explanation: You merge into the branch you currently have checked out.

questions.question: What is a merge commit?
options: A commit with exactly one parent
A commit with two parents joining histories
questions.explanation: A merge commit connects two lines of history.

questions.question: Why is visualizing branches useful?
questions.explanation: Seeing the graph makes branch movement and merges easier to reason about.

codingChallenge.title: Merge feature back to main
codingChallenge.description: Simulate a full branch cycle: commit on main, commit on feature, then merge into main.
codingChallenge.starterCode:
# Build this flow:
# main commit -> feature commit -> merge feature into main

testCases.input: Goal: end on main with a merge commit, while feature still points to its latest feature commit.
testCases.expectedOutput:
HEAD=main
HAS_BRANCH=main
HAS_BRANCH=feature
MIN_COMMITS=4
BRANCH_AT=feature:C2
BRANCH_AT=main:C3
MERGE_COMMIT_ON=main

codingChallenge.hint: Do commits on both branches first, then checkout main and merge feature.
codingChallenge.solution:
git commit -m "Base on main"
git branch feature
git checkout feature
git commit -m "Feature commit"
git checkout main
git merge feature

lessons.title: Beginner Branch Workflow Mission
lessons.description: Practice an end-to-end branch workflow using checkout -b and merge

theorySlides.title: Daily Workflow Pattern
theorySlides.content:
A practical beginner flow:

1) Start from main
2) Create branch with checkout -b
3) Commit feature work
4) Return to main
5) Merge branch

theorySlides.title: Why this works
theorySlides.content: This workflow keeps changes focused, reviewable, and easy to rollback if needed.

theorySlides.title: Mission Commands
theorySlides.content: Use this exact idea in your final beginner challenge.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
git commit -m "Main baseline"
git checkout -b bugfix
git commit -m "Fix issue"
git checkout main
git commit -m "Main update"
git merge bugfix

questions.question: What is the best command to create and switch branches fast?
questions.explanation: checkout -b combines branch creation and branch switch.

questions.question: In this workflow, when do you merge?
options: After feature branch has meaningful commits
questions.explanation: You merge after implementing and committing feature work.

questions.question: Why commit on main before merge in this mission?
options: To create diverging histories for realistic merge practice
questions.explanation: A realistic merge often joins two branches that both moved forward.

questions.question: What should you verify after merge?
questions.explanation: Check branch pointers and commit graph to confirm workflow correctness.
